cards.title: Attention Is Not What You Need (2025)

depth.text: someone proposes an **attention-free model** that tracks **token pairs** through geometric subspaces instead of an attention matrix

Its Causal Grassmann layer encodes local token pairs as **two-dimensional subspaces**, then mixes those features back into the model. On Wikitext-2, models with 13 to 18 million parameters came **within about 10 to 15 percent** of size-matched Transformers on validation perplexity; on SNLI, a Grassmann-Plucker head on DistilBERT **slightly outperformed** a Transformer head.

cards.camps: Two camps: some see attention-free methods as useful alternatives, especially on small sequences; others call the tests too small and flag a possible token-pairing bug and unresolved compute costs.

comments.text: The author describes the model's pairing operation as: (zt,zt+Delta) where Delta is a positive offset. This means the model is using the next token to predict the next token. It should have been (zt,zt-Delta), or it's cheating. I don't know if that's just the paper, or if the code was also b0rk3d.

I agree with the framing but the claim is too strong. I don't think Grassmannian manifolds are necessarily a better representation than simple query/key inner products. It's a valid solution, and it does have advantages in some cases. The Grassmannian is only preserving the subspace orientation, so we lose information about the actual linear map and basically throw out its basis. Like everything…

My gut (informed by 30ish years of professional hardware and software engineering) says implemented at scale, on a real machine, we start seeing the same performance issues functional languages have where absolute conformity to the math will increase latency. Tis why Haskell, etc, will not be used to write a meaningful OS wielded at scale. Graphics mutations don't want to wait for long dead Mr…

Scale is all you need. That's why you see other attention free large language models work. But in a world with constraints on time and compute the architecture does matter because scaling does have a cost (which is dropping)
There are many alternatives to attention which work well for small sequence sizes.

The author reports throughput rising from **5.1MP/s** to **11.2MP/s** in testing. To make unsigned pixel values fit the chip’s signed comparisons, the code XORs each loaded value with **0x80**.

cards.camps: Two camps: the article calls it a 220% improvement; a commenter says that's a 120% increase, or 2.2x faster.

comments.text: BTW, I find it pretty amazing that you can buy complete ESP32-S3-Zero boards on AliExpress for $5.33. That's for a little board with the chip, a ceramic antenna, a USB connector and an LED. ESP32-C3-Zero are $2.80 each. These prices are absolutely ridiculous for what you get. Also, the ease of use of these boards is incredible. Just connect them via USB to your computer and off you go.
> For its price, the ESP32-S3 is a powerhouse of a microcontroller. Indeed, don't forget it is more powerful than computers like this one, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amstrad_PC1512
nit: 5.1MP/s to 11.2MP/s is not an increase of 220%, it's an increase of 120%. it's 2.2x faster, but percentage increase starts at 0%, not 100%. 100% faster is double, 200% faster is triple.

The engineering seems impressive, but how useful is the result? What can you detect exactly with it in real time? Detecting corners, but to what resolution/detail, a picture with a result would have been helpful to understand the capability. edit: missed this link, this is what this is about https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Features_from_accelerated_segm...

The CH32V407/CH32V467 is a bit more expensive, was $2.4 per unit two month ago, but supports the embedded subset of the RISC-V vector extension. So you basically get a full AVX-512/SVE level SIMD ISA, minus FP support and with 64-bit SIMD width. But you still have LMUL, which will be great here to maximize utilization.

glossary.firmware: The built-in software that tells a device's hardware how to work.
glossary.POC: Proof of Concept: a small test or demo that checks whether an idea can work.
glossary.MRI: Magnetic resonance imaging: a scan that uses magnets to make pictures of the inside of the body.
glossary.neuroplasticity: The brain’s ability to change how it works and is organised over time.
glossary.cognitive decline: A worsening ability to remember, think clearly or follow a conversation.
glossary.confounding factor: Something else that may explain a result, making it hard to know what caused it.
glossary.MCP: Model Context Protocol: a standard way for AI apps to connect to outside tools.
glossary.REST: A common way for one app to send requests to another app over a network.
glossary.OCR: Optical character recognition: software that reads words from a picture or scanned page.
glossary.PII: Personally Identifiable Information: details that could identify someone, such as an email or phone number.
glossary.WASM: WebAssembly: a way for an app to run plug-ins written in other programming languages.
glossary.Rust: A programming language; commenters say 37signals used it for the Hey backend.
glossary.S-1: A filing that gives investors details about a company's finances and share offering before an IPO.
glossary.open-weight models: AI models whose learned settings are made available for others to use or change.
glossary.compute: The processing power computers use to run AI or other software.
glossary.net loss: When a company spends more than it earns over a reporting period.
glossary.operating profit: Money left from a company's main business after its operating costs are paid.
glossary.stock-based compensation: Paying workers partly with shares in the company instead of cash.
glossary.IPO: Initial Public Offering: when a company first offers its shares for the public to buy.
glossary.Lighthouse: A tool that checks a web page’s speed and other quality measures.
glossary.framework: A collection of ready-made parts and rules that helps people build software.
glossary.static site: A website made of ready-to-serve pages, rather than pages generated anew for each visit.
glossary.CDN: Content Delivery Network: A network of servers that helps websites handle requests closer to their users.
glossary.ISR: Incremental Static Regeneration: a way to refresh already-built pages after a site is published.
glossary.hydration: JavaScript adding the behavior that makes a page’s controls work after its HTML loads.
glossary.server components: Parts of a website that run on the site’s server instead of in a visitor’s browser.
glossary.SEO: Search engine optimization: making changes to a webpage so it is more likely to appear in search results.
glossary.NeXTSTEP: The main software that ran NeXT computers and gave people the screens and tools they used.
glossary.sequence: A section of a film made up of several shots.
glossary.shot: A stretch of a film made with one camera setup.
glossary.frame: One still picture in a film; shown quickly with others, it looks like movement.
glossary.stereo 3D: A way to show different images to the left and right eyes so the picture looks deep.
glossary.pipeline: A series of steps where each step works on data and passes it to the next.
glossary.rig: A setup that lets animators move a digital character.
glossary.FTP: File Transfer Protocol: a way to move files between your computer and a server.
glossary.webmail: Email you use through a website instead of an app on your device.
glossary.DNS: Domain Name System: the internet's address book, which helps a computer find a website from its name.
glossary.ISP: Internet Service Provider: a company that connects people to the internet.
glossary.VPN: Virtual private network: a service that sends your internet traffic through another computer, often to protect it or make it appear to come from somewhere else.
glossary.DoH: DNS over HTTPS: a way to send website-name lookups through a protected web connection.
glossary.DoT: DNS over TLS: a way to protect website-name lookups as they travel over the internet.
glossary.run-off election: An extra election round where voters choose between candidates after an earlier round leaves no winner.
glossary.inference provider: A service that runs an AI model and sends its replies to an app.
glossary.cache read: Reusing saved text from earlier in a conversation instead of processing it all over again.
glossary.grading on completion: A teacher checks whether you turned the work in, rather than whether every answer is right.
glossary.AI agents: Computer programs that can carry out tasks, rather than only answer a question.
glossary.git worktree: A separate working copy of a project, so you can work on another task without mixing up files.
glossary.living specs: Project notes that describe what the software is meant to do and are updated as it changes.
glossary.CLI: Command-Line Interface: a way to control a computer by typing commands instead of clicking buttons.
glossary.pi: The coding agent ThinkRail runs to work on code.
glossary.mRNA: Messenger RNA: instructions that cells can use to make proteins.
glossary.Phase 3 trial: A later-stage test in people that compares a treatment with the usual care or another option.
glossary.intismeran: The name of the personalized mRNA vaccine used with Keytruda in this trial.
glossary.Keytruda: Merck’s cancer treatment used as the standard treatment in this trial.
glossary.placebo: A treatment with no active study drug, used so researchers can compare it with the drug being tested.
glossary.RFS: Recurrence-free survival: how long a patient goes without the cancer returning.
glossary.DMFS: Distant metastasis-free survival: how long a patient goes without the cancer returning in a different part of the body.
glossary.monoclonal antibody: A lab-made medicine designed to latch onto one particular target in the body.
glossary.BBS: Bulletin Board System: an online place people used to post messages and share files.
glossary.cracktro: A short intro that plays before a game, made by people who cracked its copy protection.
glossary.demo: A short computer-made display of visual effects, made to show what its creators can do.
glossary.demoscene: A community where people make computer demos to show off skill and creativity.
glossary.Hex View: A way to see a file's contents as numbers and change them.
glossary.Pascal: A programming language used in Denthor's tutorials.
glossary.ordered map: A collection that stores items in a chosen order and lets a program find one by its label.
glossary.B-tree: A way of keeping sorted items in a tree-shaped layout so a program can find them quickly.
glossary.trie: A way to organize words by their shared beginnings so software can find matching words quickly.
glossary.DRAM: Dynamic Random-Access Memory: the working memory a computer uses while running things.
